info.text: The three things a film is built from at once: what the camera captures, how the pieces are joined, and the story that both are serving.

clusters.name: Cinematography
clusters.fact: Cinematography is what happens in front of the camera and to it: how close it stands, from what angle, and everything arranged within the frame.

camera angle.text: Where the camera is placed relative to the subject -- high, low, or level -- which shapes how powerful or vulnerable that subject looks.

close-up.text: A shot tight enough to fill the screen with a face or a single detail, used to draw out emotion.

mise-en-scène.text: Everything arranged in front of the camera for a shot: setting, lighting, costume, and the placement of actors.

wide shot.text: A shot distant enough to show a person's whole body and much of the space around them; also called a long shot.

clusters.name: Editing
clusters.fact: Editing decides how shots meet: an ordinary cut joins them invisibly, continuity editing keeps dozens of cuts feeling like unbroken time and space, and a jump cut or a montage breaks that continuity on purpose.

continuity editing.text: The standard practice of cutting shots together so that time and space feel unbroken to the viewer.

cut.text: The basic edit: one shot ends and the next begins, instantly.

jump cut.text: A cut that breaks continuity on purpose, visibly skipping time within what looks like a single ongoing shot.

montage.text: A rapid sequence of shots that compresses time or builds an idea, rather than showing events in real time.

clusters.name: Narrative
clusters.fact: Narrative is the story itself: a protagonist pursuing something across a plot, in whatever genre the film belongs to, filtered through whoever is telling it.

genre.text: A category of film defined by shared conventions of story, style, or mood, such as the western or the musical.

narrator.text: Whoever's perspective is telling the story, and how much that perspective knows.

plot.text: The sequence of events, and how one causes the next, that the story is built from.

protagonist.text: The character whose goals and choices the story follows most closely.

bridges.fact: A point-of-view shot is a camera placement decision -- literally an angle -- built for a single purpose: putting the audience inside one character's perspective on the story.

info.text: A shot positioned to show the audience exactly what one character sees.

bridges.fact: Shots joined by continuity editing accumulate into a scene, and the scene -- not the shot -- is the unit the plot actually advances through.

info.text: A section of a film in one place and continuous time, built from a series of shots.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts are decided by how a single shot is composed, before it's ever joined to another shot?
lenses.explanation: All five are choices made about one shot in isolation -- how close the camera stands, where it's placed, what's arranged for it to see, and whose perspective it's built to represent. None describes a relationship between two shots; that's the next round.

reasons.camera angle: Where the camera is positioned relative to the subject in this one shot.
reasons.close-up: How close the camera stands to the subject in this one shot.
reasons.mise-en-scène: Everything arranged in front of the camera for this one shot to capture.
reasons.point-of-view shot: A specific camera angle chosen to put the audience inside a character's perspective, decided shot by shot.
reasons.wide shot: How far back the camera stands in this one shot.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts describe how one shot relates to the next, rather than what's inside any single shot?
lenses.explanation: These are all about the seam between shots -- whether it's invisible, intentionally jarring, or compressed into a rapid sequence -- and about what accumulates once shots are joined. None can be judged by looking at a single frozen frame.

reasons.continuity editing: The practice of making a whole sequence of cuts feel unbroken.
reasons.cut: The instantaneous join between one shot and the next.
reasons.jump cut: A cut that deliberately breaks that unbroken feeling.
reasons.montage: A rapid sequence of shots joined to compress time or build an idea.
reasons.scene: What accumulates once shots are joined by continuity editing into one place and time.

lenses.prompt: Which concept is the raw material or basic reference point that everything else in its area is built from or filtered through?
lenses.explanation: Every other cinematography term describes a way of showing what's arranged in the mise-en-scène; every other editing term describes a variation on the plain cut; and every other narrative element -- protagonist, plot, genre -- reaches the audience only through whoever the narrator is. One per area, and each is the thing the rest of its area is defined against.

reasons.cut: Continuity editing, the jump cut, and the montage are all variations on this same basic join.
reasons.mise-en-scène: Close-ups, wide shots, and camera angles are all just different ways of showing what's arranged in the mise-en-scène.
reasons.narrator: Everything else in the story -- who it follows, what happens, what genre it belongs to -- reaches the audience through this filter.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts are a single structure built by combining smaller parts, rather than a technique used to build something or a single primitive?
lenses.explanation: A shot's mise-en-scène is a combination of setting, lighting, costume, and blocking; a montage combines many shots; a scene combines shots joined by continuity editing; a plot combines causally connected events. Continuity editing and cut are excluded on purpose -- they're the methods used to do the combining, not the resulting structure.

reasons.mise-en-scène: Combines setting, lighting, costume, and actor placement into one visual whole.
reasons.montage: Combines a rapid sequence of individual shots into one unit.
reasons.plot: Combines individual events, linked by cause and effect, into the story's throughline.
reasons.scene: Combines shots joined by continuity editing into one place and time.
